169 DISCOVERIES · ONE LAKEFRONT

Follow your curiosity.

A hidden pocket of birdsong. A grand old beach house. A skyline you’ve never seen quite this way. There’s a place for every kind of wander.

BEACH

Sand, sky & a place to pause.

On the trail

Kathy Osterman Beach

A generous crescent of pale sand, neighborhood picnics, and a horizon that seems to go on forever.

Locals also call this Hollywood Beach, after the nearby avenue.

Check the Park District’s daily swimming status and posted lifeguard hours.

On the map ↗The story ↗

Photo: Alanscottwalker · CC BY-SA 3.0 ↗

On the trail

Foster Beach

Lawn becomes sand, sand becomes lake. Foster is an easy place to let a short stop become an afternoon.

The beach is part of Lincoln Park’s long North Side landscape.

Use designated beach access paths and check daily swimming conditions.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Photo: Alanscottwalker · CC BY 3.0 ↗

Via a connector

Montrose Dog Beach

A separate stretch of sand at Montrose welcomes dogs and their people beside the lake.

The official dog-friendly area occupies the north end of Montrose Beach.

Dogs require the Park District permit and tag. Follow the posted dog-area rules and keep dogs out of nearby bird habitat.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Photo: TonyTheTiger (t/c/bio/WP:CHICAGO/WP:LOTM) · CC BY-SA 3.0 ↗

Via a connector

Montrose Beach

An expansive beach where volleyball nets and lake breezes give way to protected dunes and bird habitat.

Montrose’s dunes and neighboring sanctuary create an unusually rich urban habitat.

Respect fenced nesting areas. Dogs are allowed only in the designated dog-friendly area.

On the map ↗The story ↗

Photo: User:JeremyA · CC BY-SA 2.5 ↗

On the trail

North Avenue Beach

The Chicago postcard comes into focus: sand, volleyball courts, a ship-shaped beach house, and towers beyond.

The beach house’s silhouette evokes an ocean liner.

Slow down at beach crossings. Swimming and concessions have seasonal schedules.

On the map ↗The story ↗

Photo: King of Hearts · CC BY-SA 3.0 ↗

On the trail

Oak Street Beach

The Gold Coast meets the sand. Few places put beach towels and skyscrapers quite this close together.

The shoreline bends dramatically here toward the downtown waterfront.

The exposed lake edge can be affected by wind and waves. Follow signs and official notices.

On the map ↗The story ↗

Photo: Adam Jones, Ph.D. · CC BY-SA 3.0 ↗

On the trail

Ohio Street Beach

A small pocket of sand tucked beside Streeterville, with Navy Pier just around the corner.

Ohio Street Beach sits beside the peninsula containing Olive Park.

Check official beach conditions; watch for swimmers and pedestrians at beach approaches.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Photo: David Wilson from Oak Park, Illinois, USA · CC BY 2.0 ↗

Nearby detour

12th Street Beach

A sheltered sand beach sits just south of Adler Planetarium on Northerly Island.

The beach is separate from the natural area farther south on the peninsula.

Swimming is seasonal and limited to designated areas when lifeguards are on duty; check current conditions.

Photo: DwightSchruteDunderMifflin · CC BY 4.0 ↗

On the trail

Margaret T. Burroughs Beach

At 31st Street, turn back toward the city: the skyline stretches across the water beyond sand and sailboats.

The beach honors artist, educator, and DuSable Museum co-founder Margaret T. Burroughs.

Also called 31st Street Beach. Check official swimming conditions and signed neighborhood connections.

Photo: Brian Kay · CC BY 3.0 ↗

On the trail

Oakwood Beach

An open stretch of South Side sand, with room to pause between Burnham Park’s longer trail sections.

Oakwood Beach is reached from the 41st Street area.

Use the designated neighborhood connector and check current swimming conditions.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

On the trail

57th Street Beach

Hyde Park’s sweep of sand, a short distance from the Point and the grand museum across the drive.

The beach sits near the northern edge of Jackson Park.

Use signed crossings for inland destinations and check daily swimming conditions.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

The beach house at 57th Street Beach.

On the trail

63rd Street Beach

A generous beach and a Classical Revival pavilion bring a graceful sense of arrival to the southern shore.

Completed in 1919, the beach house has open-air galleries designed to catch lake breezes.

Check beach conditions and seasonal facility access before visiting.

On the map ↗The story ↗

Photo: User:TonyTheTiger · CC BY-SA 3.0 ↗

Via a connector

South Shore Beach

A small swimming beach lies east of the South Shore Cultural Center, beside its nature sanctuary.

The beach belongs to the Cultural Center park, a separate place from the historic clubhouse.

Swimming is seasonal when lifeguards are on duty; follow current beach conditions and posted access.

NATURE

A quieter kind of Chicago.

On the trail

Osterman Beach Dunes

Native dune grasses frame the northern end of the trail beside Osterman Beach.

Marram grass helps trap sand and stabilize this restored shoreline habitat.

Observe the dunes from bordering beach walks and trails; stay outside planted habitat.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

On the trail

Foster Beach Dunes

Small native plantings bring dune habitat into the paths around Foster Beach.

The Park District identifies marram grass and silverweed among the plantings.

Use the paved trail and designated soft-surface paths; avoid trampling the dune plants.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Nearby detour

Montrose Beach Dunes

Dunes and low wetland habitat occupy the eastern end of Montrose Beach, beyond the open recreational sand.

The Park District stopped grooming this area in 2001, allowing dune and rare panne habitat to develop.

Follow posted protection zones; the paths are sandy, with paved viewing routes along the south edge and pier.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Photo: Raed Mansour · CC BY 2.0 ↗

Nearby detour

Cricket Hill

A rare little rise in a famously flat city, with grass underfoot and wide sky overhead.

The grassy hill sits inland of Montrose Beach in Lincoln Park.

Reach it on local park paths; expect people enjoying the slopes.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Photo: FHKE · CC BY-SA 2.0 ↗

Nearby detour

Montrose Point Bird Sanctuary

Step into the Magic Hedge. The skyline recedes, and the smallest movement in the leaves becomes the main event.

More than 300 bird species have been recorded in the sanctuary and adjacent dunes.

Explore on foot, stay on marked paths, and observe birds at a distance.

On the map ↗The story ↗

Photo: Theemausoliam · CC BY-SA 4.0 ↗

Nearby detour

Lincoln Park Peace Garden

A small garden of native plants offers a quiet break near the Buena Park lakefront.

The Park District, Greenpeace Great Lakes and Uptown residents renovated this former rock garden in the mid-1980s.

Explore on the garden paths without stepping into the native planting beds.

Chicago Park District sign at the Lincoln Park Peace Garden

Nearby detour

Bill Jarvis Migratory Bird Sanctuary

A protected bird habitat between Belmont Harbor and the Waveland playing fields.

The sanctuary is one of the Park District sites where volunteers monitor purple martin nesting towers.

Use surrounding public paths and respect the sanctuary’s posted habitat boundaries.

Wetland habitat at Bill Jarvis Migratory Bird Sanctuary · 2010

On the trail

AIDS Garden Chicago

A lakefront garden of remembrance south of Belmont Harbor, marked by Keith Haring’s vivid green Self-Portrait.

The garden occupies the former Belmont Rocks gathering place and honors those affected by Chicago’s HIV epidemic.

Walk through the garden on its paths and give people space for quiet reflection.

Signed benches and garden entrance at AIDS Garden Chicago

Nearby detour

Diversey Natural Area

Native grasses and wetland plants fill a pocket of habitat just north of Diversey Harbor.

The Park District converted this often-flooded lawn into prairie, savanna and wetland habitat that also retains stormwater.

Use the paved path along the west side and respect posted habitat boundaries.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Nearby detour

North Pond

A quiet loop of water and reeds with neighborhood towers reflected among the trees.

The pond is inland in Lincoln Park, west of the lakefront route.

Use designated park paths and roadway crossings for this inland detour.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Photo: Bohao Zhao · CC BY 3.0 ↗

Nearby detour

Alfred Caldwell Lily Pool

Layered limestone, native planting, and a still pool make a small world within the city.

Alfred Caldwell’s Prairie-style landscape is a National Historic Landmark.

Nearby detour

Lincoln Park Conservatory

Step under glass into palms, ferns and changing flower displays in the middle of Lincoln Park.

The conservatory was built in stages from 1890 to 1895 and contains four display houses.

Check current reservations and opening hours before visiting the indoor gardens.

Nearby detour

Grandmother’s Garden

A long garden border along Stockton Drive invites a slower walk beside the conservatory grounds.

The Park District identifies this garden at Stockton Drive and Webster Avenue, extending across three blocks.

Stay on the garden paths and allow room for other visitors stopping to look at the planting.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Nearby detour

South Pond · Nature Boardwalk

A boardwalk circuit through prairie and wetland planting, with the city skyline reflected in South Pond.

Lincoln Park Zoo opened the restored Nature Boardwalk habitat in 2010.

Follow the boardwalk and park paths; keep wildlife and shoreline planting undisturbed.

Photo: Alanscottwalker · CC BY-SA 3.0 ↗

Nearby detour

Milton Lee Olive Park

Lakeside lawns and paths north of Navy Pier offer a broad view back toward Chicago’s towers.

The park is named in honor of Milton Lee Olive, a Chicago-born Medal of Honor recipient.

On the trail

Jane Addams Memorial Natural Area

A pocket of native prairie sits just south of Ohio Street Beach, close to Navy Pier.

Interpretive signs introduce nature in the city beside the prairie plantings.

Polk Bros Park

Lawns, paths and a fountain form Navy Pier’s green front door.

This 13-acre public space includes outdoor performance lawns and was transformed through the Polk family’s 2014 gift.

Check Navy Pier’s current program and fountain information when planning a visit.

Cancer Survivors’ Garden

A contemplative garden occupies the eastern edge of Maggie Daley Park beneath tall granite columns.

Completed in 1996, its garden rooms express acceptance, support and celebration.

Maggie Daley Park

A playful downtown landscape of climbing, skating, and paths that rise and turn among the lawns.

The curving BP Pedestrian Bridge connects this park to Millennium Park.

Lurie Garden

Northerly Island

McCormick Bird Sanctuary

Native prairie and woodland create a bird habitat beside McCormick Place and the lakefront.

Part of its prairie grows above an underground parking garage.

Use the overlook off the trail and designated paths; stay outside fenced habitat.

Burnham Nature Sanctuary

On the trail

Burnham Park

Long lawns, lake breezes, and an uninterrupted sense of the city stretching south.

Much of this lakefront park was created through landfill and successive public works projects.

Bring water and plan your access point before choosing a longer section.

Lakefront promenade near McCormick Place Bird Sanctuary.

Cornell Garden Oasis

Promontory Point

A peninsula of mature trees and limestone steps, with the city a distant silhouette across the lake.

Alfred Caldwell designed the Point’s Prairie-style landscape in 1937.

Osaka Garden · Garden of the Phoenix

Bobolink Meadow

Jackson Park & Wooded Island

Lagoons, birdsong, and the Garden of the Phoenix reveal a quieter, inland chapter of the lakefront.

Jackson Park was a principal site of the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition.

63rd Street Beach Dunes

Native grasses and shoreline plants form habitat on either side of the swimming beach.

The natural area supports migrating birds along the southern lakefront.

South Shore Nature Sanctuary

South Shore Formal Garden

HARBOR

Follow the masts.

Montrose Harbor

A sheltered curl of water, a forest of masts, and an ever-changing view of boats slipping out to the lake.

The harbor sits on the sheltered side of the Montrose peninsula.

Belmont Harbor

Burnham Harbor

31st Street Harbor

59th Street Harbor

Jackson Park Outer Harbor

LANDMARK

Stories written in the skyline.

On the trail

Ardmore Avenue

Your north-to-south journey begins where Edgewater meets Lake Michigan. The whole shoreline lies ahead.

The official northern end of the Lakefront Trail is Ardmore Avenue.

Find the signed walking and cycling paths at the beach approach.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Photo: AlphaBeta135 · CC BY-SA 4.0 ↗

On the trail

Come to Light

Glittering tile and glass wrap the old Osterman Beach comfort station in images of planets, water and wildlife.

Andy Bellomo led the community mosaic project, completed in 2011.

View the mosaic from the surrounding paths; the artwork is on the old comfort station, not the newer beach house.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Dr. José Rizal Monument

A bronze memorial beside Marine Drive honors the Filipino writer, physician and independence figure.

Antonio T. Mondejar’s Chicago sculpture was unveiled in 1999 as a replica of his monument in Dapitan, Philippines.

Waveland Clock Tower

A distinctive clock tower gives the open north lakefront a recognizable meeting point.

Kwa-Ma-Rolas · Kwanusila

On the trail

Mermaid · La Sirena

A reclining mermaid carved into limestone rests near 41st Street, with Lake Michigan behind her.

Chicago artists carved the figure into lakefront stone in 1986; it moved to this landscaped setting in 2010.

Find the artwork from the paved lakefront paths; avoid climbing the sculpture.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

On the trail

David Wallach Memorial Fountain

A small bronze fawn rests above a polished stone fountain at the approach to Promontory Point.

Elisabeth Haseltine Hibbard sculpted the fawn and Frederick Hibbard designed the fountain, installed in 1939.

Look east of the 55th Street underpass; do not rely on the fountain for drinking water without checking it on site.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Via a connector

Griffin Museum of Science and Industry

The surviving Palace of Fine Arts from the 1893 fair is now a monumental home for science and discovery.

The building began as the Palace of Fine Arts at the World’s Columbian Exposition.

Check admission and hours; use designated park and lakefront connections.

Nearby detour

Sky Landing

A cluster of silver lotus petals rises from the lawn near the Japanese garden on Wooded Island.

Yoko Ono installed this twelve-petal sculpture in 2016 as a symbol of peace.

Reach it on Wooded Island’s paths using designated bridges and road crossings.

Nearby detour

Obama Presidential Center

A museum and public campus occupy the western edge of Jackson Park along Stony Island Avenue.

The campus combines museum exhibits, public art, gardens and a Chicago Public Library branch.

The campus has free public spaces; the museum requires a timed ticket. Use the operator’s current visitor information and designated park crossings.

On the trail

63rd Street Beach House

Long arcades and courtyards make this historic bathing pavilion a landmark beside the sand.

The pavilion was constructed by 1919 and restored in 2000.

Check seasonal facility access and event reservations; this pin identifies the building, not the swimming beach.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Photo: User:TonyTheTiger · CC BY-SA 3.0 ↗

Nearby detour

Statue of the Republic

The gilded figure known as the Golden Lady stands at Hayes and Richards Drives in Jackson Park.

Daniel Chester French’s 1918 statue is a smaller commemorative version of the one made for the 1893 exposition.

Use designated crossings to approach the monument; the pin is on the statue itself.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

Photo: Marlin Keesler · CC BY 2.0 ↗

Via a connector

Jackson Harbor Station

A historic lifesaving station survives beside Jackson Park’s outer harbor, a small reminder of the lake’s working past.

The surviving station house was built in 1908 to a design by Victor Mindeleff.

View the exterior from public harbor paths; check current building access before entering.

Nearby detour

South Shore Cultural Center

A former country club, now a cultural landmark, set among lawns and a long view of the lake.

The cultural center occupies the former South Shore Country Club.

Building hours and event access differ from park access. Follow public paths.

On the map ↗The story ↗

Photo: Zol87 from Chicago, IL, USA · CC BY-SA 4.0 ↗

Nearby detour

Paul Robeson Theatre

A named performance venue forms part of the South Shore Cultural Center complex.

The Park District lists the theatre at the Cultural Center’s 7059 South Shore Drive address.

Check scheduled performances or rental access; this is an indoor venue, not an always-open trail facility.

On the map ↗Visitor information ↗

On the trail

71st Street · The southern end

Eighteen miles of lakefront behind you. A whole city of discoveries to come back for.

71st Street is the official southern endpoint of the Lakefront Trail.

Plan onward travel separately from the trail, using current transit or street navigation.
